tagline: The visions, sign-acts, and oracles of a priest exiled to Babylon, who saw God's glory leave Jerusalem's temple and saw it return.
overview:
Ezekiel was a priest who never served in the temple. He was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and five years later, living among the exiles beside the Kebar canal, he saw the heavens open and the glory of the LORD come to him in a foreign land. For the next twenty years or more he spoke to a displaced community that clung to the hope that Jerusalem could not fall and that their stay in Babylon would be short. His first task was to destroy that hope. His second, after the city fell in 587 or 586 BC, was to give them a better one.

The book is full of strange and memorable things: a vision of living creatures, wheels, and a throne above a crystal expanse; a scroll eaten like honey; a prophet who lies on his side for months beside a clay model of a besieged city; the glory of God rising from the temple and departing east; a valley of dry bones that stands up as an army; and a final vision of a new temple from which a river flows out to heal the Dead Sea. Behind all of it is one conviction repeated more than sixty times: that people and nations will know that I am the LORD.

Ezekiel matters because it shows God's holiness and his faithfulness at the same moment. God judges his people because he is holy and will not share his house with idols. He restores them for the same reason, for the sake of his holy name, and he promises what they cannot produce themselves: a new heart, a new spirit, and his own presence dwelling among them again.
author:
The book presents itself as the work of Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest (1:3), and most of it is written in the first person with precise dates. Jewish and Christian tradition has accepted it as his. A line in the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says the men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel, which most take to mean that a later body put the collection into its final written form, not that they composed it.

In the early twentieth century some critical scholars assigned large parts of the book to later writers. Most scholars today credit the core of the book to the prophet himself, though they differ on how much later shaping it received. Walther Zimmerli, in his major commentary, argued that disciples of Ezekiel extended and applied his words in a kind of school. Moshe Greenberg, in his commentary, argued that the book reads best as a coherent composition largely from the prophet's own hand. Both views take the dates, the setting, and the prophet's voice seriously.
date: Ezekiel is the most carefully dated of the prophetic books. More than a dozen oracles carry a date counted from the exile of King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The first vision comes in the fifth year of that exile, in the summer of 593 BC (1:2). News of Jerusalem's fall reaches the exiles in the twelfth year (33:21). The temple vision is dated to the twenty-fifth year, about 573 BC (40:1), and the latest dated oracle, a short word about Egypt, to the twenty-seventh year, about 571 BC (29:17). The book was probably gathered into its present form during the exile, soon after its last oracle, though scholars who see more editorial expansion allow for a longer process. The thirtieth year in 1:1 is unexplained; many take it as the prophet's age when he was called.
setting:
Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II was the great power of the day. In 597 BC it took King Jehoiachin, the royal family, officials, soldiers, and craftsmen into exile (2 Kings 24:10-16), and Ezekiel went with them. The exiles were settled in communities in southern Mesopotamia, including Tel-abib by the Kebar canal (3:15). Babylonian business records from the city of Nippur mention a canal by the name Kabar, which is probably the same waterway. The exiles had their own houses and elders (8:1) and some freedom to gather, but they were far from the land and the temple.

Back in Jerusalem, King Zedekiah ruled as a Babylonian vassal and was soon plotting rebellion with Egypt's help. Prophets in both places promised a quick deliverance. Ezekiel, like Jeremiah in Jerusalem, insisted that the city would fall, and in 587 or 586 BC it did. His later oracles address a community that has lost everything it had trusted: city, king, land, and temple. They also address the nations around Judah, especially Tyre and Egypt, whose pride and opportunism the prophet judges.
purpose: Ezekiel's book had two jobs, one before the fall of Jerusalem and one after. Before the fall, it aimed to strip the exiles of false confidence: the temple would not save a city that had filled it with idols, and God was not bound to a building. The famous vision of the glory leaving the temple (chapters 8 to 11) makes that point. After the fall, the book aimed to keep the survivors from despair by showing that the same God who judged would restore, not because Israel deserved it but for the sake of his name. It also calls every hearer to personal responsibility (chapter 18) and to the hope of a new heart and spirit given by God (chapter 36).
story: Ezekiel belongs to the exile, the long gap between the fall of Jerusalem (told in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah) and the return under Persian rule (told in Ezra and Nehemiah). He is a younger contemporary of Jeremiah and an older contemporary of Daniel, whom he mentions by name (14:14; 28:3). Where Jeremiah watched the end from inside Jerusalem and Lamentations mourned it, Ezekiel interpreted it from Babylon. His visions of a restored people, a united kingdom under a Davidic shepherd, and a renewed temple shaped the hopes of the returning exiles and, in turn, the imagery of the New Testament.
christ: Several of Ezekiel's great promises come to rest in Jesus. In chapter 34 God condemns the shepherds who fed themselves, promises to shepherd his flock himself, and in the same breath promises one shepherd, his servant David; Jesus calls himself the good shepherd in John 10 against that background. The promise of a new heart and a new spirit within (36:26-27) belongs with Jeremiah's new covenant, and the New Testament sees it fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit. The glory that left the temple returns, and John says of Jesus that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us and that we saw his glory (John 1:14). The river from the temple becomes Jesus' picture of the Spirit flowing from within believers (John 7:37-39) and Revelation's river of the water of life (Revelation 22:1-2). Ezekiel's title, son of man, mostly means simply a mortal, and the New Testament's use of that title for Jesus draws more directly on Daniel 7; but the humble prophet who bears his people's iniquity in chapter 4 is a real, if partial, pattern of the one who would bear it fully.
reading:
Ezekiel mixes several kinds of writing: visions (chapters 1 to 3, 8 to 11, 37, and 40 to 48), sign-acts in which the prophet acts out his message, long allegories (chapters 16, 17, 23), legal-style case teaching (chapter 18), oracles against nations, and detailed architectural description. Take each on its own terms. The visions use deliberately cautious language (the likeness of, the appearance of) and are not meant to be drawn as diagrams. The allegories of chapters 16 and 23 use harsh sexual imagery for idolatry; they shock on purpose, and readers should notice that they condemn the people's unfaithfulness, not women as such.

Watch for the dates, which place each oracle in the unfolding crisis, and for the refrains: son of man, they will know that I am the LORD, and the glory of the LORD. Follow the glory through the book: it appears by the Kebar (chapter 1), departs from the temple toward the east (chapters 10 and 11), and returns from the east to fill a new temple (43:1-5). That movement is the book's spine. Jewish tradition treated chapter 1 and the closing temple vision with special caution, and readers today should resist two opposite errors: dismissing the visions as unintelligible, and filling them with speculative detail the text doesn't give.

structure.title: The call by the Kebar canal
structure.summary: Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD on a mobile throne, is commissioned as a prophet to a rebellious house, eats a scroll, and is appointed a watchman.

structure.title: Judgment on Jerusalem
structure.summary: Sign-acts and oracles announce the siege and fall of the city. In a vision the prophet sees idolatry in the temple and watches the glory of God depart. Allegories, case law on responsibility, and laments follow, ending on the day the siege begins and the prophet's wife dies.

structure.title: Oracles against the nations
structure.summary: Judgment on Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and above all Egypt, nations that gloated over Judah or trusted in their own power.

structure.title: Restoration promised
structure.summary: After news of the city's fall, the prophet's mouth is opened. God promises a true shepherd, a new heart and spirit, the resurrection of the nation from dry bones, the reunion of Israel and Judah, and final victory over Gog.

structure.title: The new temple and the returning glory
structure.summary: A vision of a restored temple and land. The glory of the LORD returns from the east, a river flows from the sanctuary to bring life, and the city is named The LORD is there.

themes.title: The holiness and glory of God
themes.body: Ezekiel is a priest, and he sees everything in terms of holiness: what is clean and unclean, what honors God's presence and what defiles it. The glory of the LORD is the visible radiance of God's presence. Its departure from a defiled temple is the book's darkest moment, and its return to a purified one is its climax.

themes.title: They will know that I am the LORD
themes.body: The refrain appears throughout the book, after judgment and after restoration alike. The goal of God's action in history is that Israel and the nations will recognize who he is. God acts for the sake of his name, which means for the truth about himself to be seen.

themes.title: Judgment without false hope
themes.body: Ezekiel confronts the belief that God's people are safe because of their temple, city, or ancestry. His sign-acts make the coming siege vivid, and his oracles trace the guilt of Jerusalem back through its whole history. Judgment is not arbitrary; it answers idolatry, bloodshed, and injustice.

themes.title: Personal responsibility
themes.body: Against the proverb that the children suffer for their fathers' sins, Ezekiel insists that each person answers for his own life and that anyone who turns from wickedness will live (chapter 18). The watchman passages (3:16-21; 33:1-9) apply the same principle to the prophet's own duty to warn.

themes.title: New heart, new life, new presence
themes.body: The restoration Ezekiel promises goes deeper than a return to the land. God will cleanse his people, give them a heart of flesh in place of stone, put his Spirit within them, raise the nation from death, and dwell among them forever.

keyChapters.why: The inaugural vision of the glory of the LORD on a throne above the living creatures, shown to an exile far from the temple.
The glory rises from the temple and moves to its threshold and east gate, the beginning of God's departure from a defiled house.
The classic statement that each person answers for his own sin and that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls them to turn and live.
God judges Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David, the background to Jesus as the good shepherd.
The promise of cleansing, a new heart, and God's Spirit within his people, for the sake of his holy name.
The valley of dry bones: God's breath brings a dead nation to life, and two sticks become one kingdom.
The glory of the LORD returns from the east and fills the new temple, reversing the departure of chapters 10 and 11.
